titleText.es: Probablemente los mejores abrazos los dan  los mixinos, que pueden extrudir filamentos microscópicos que convierten un gran volumen de agua en baba en cuestión de segundos. ¡Una manta blandita instantánea!
titleText.en: The best hugs are probably from hagfish, which can extrude microscopic filaments that convert a huge volume of water around them to slime in seconds. Instant cozy blanket!
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish and official title attributes are preserved exactly, including the doubled space in dan  los. OCR split the two printed copies of CIENTÍFICOS, plus PROBLEMA, AUMENTADO, and ABRAZARTE, across line wraps; each remains one lexical occurrence. OCR also restored TÍO, JA, LA before the taxonomic label, and QUIERE. F. SEPTICA is an audited scientific-name exclusion.

regions.labelEs: EL PROBLEMA DE LOS CIENTÍFICOS ES QUE LE QUITÁIS LA MARAVILLA Y LA BELLEZA A TODAS LAS COSAS AL INTENTAR ANALIZARLAS

applications.exampleEs: EL PROBLEMA DE LOS CIENTÍFICOS ES QUE
applications.explanationEn: El problema opens the frame, the de phrase identifies whose problem it is, and es que introduces the situation.
The -áis ending marks the several people addressed informally in the vosotros form used mainly in Spain.

applications.exampleEs: LE QUITÁIS LA MARAVILLA Y LA BELLEZA A TODAS LAS COSAS
applications.explanationEn: Le marks the affected things before quitáis; the two nouns fill what is removed, and a todas las cosas makes the affected source explicit.
Al introduces when or by what action this happens, and intentar stays in its unchanged dictionary form.
Intentar stays unchanged after al, and analizar also stays in its dictionary form with las attached.
Las attaches to analizar and stands for the feminine plural things being analyzed.

regions.labelEs: MIS PLASMODIOS DE MOHO MUCILAGINOSO HAN AUMENTADO LA PRODUCCIÓN DE PIGMENTO MIRA ESTE COLOR AMARILLO ESTO LOS HACE RESISTENTES AL ZINC INCREÍBLE EH

applications.explanationEn: Moho and mucilaginoso form the conventional name of the organism.
Mucilaginoso follows moho in the neutral descriptive order.
Mucilaginoso uses masculine singular -o to match moho.
Han is the plural present helper and aumentado supplies the completed change.
Mira is the positive command for one familiar listener and works here as an attention getter.
Amarillo follows color in the neutral descriptive order.
Amarillo uses masculine singular -o to match color.
Los marks the plural things affected, hace supplies hacer, and resistentes names their resulting quality.

regions.labelEs: PARECE EL VÓMITO DE UN PERRO
JA SÍ EL APODO DE LA F. SEPTICA ES VÓMITO DE PERRO MOLA EH

excludedUnits.rationale: F. SEPTICA is a printed abbreviated Latin scientific name, not a Spanish lexical word occurrence.

applications.explanationEn: Es is a form of ser because vómito de perro identifies what the nickname is rather than giving a location.

regions.labelEs: MIRA OLVÍDALO EL PROBLEMA DE LOS CIENTÍFICOS ES QUE LE VEIS LA MARAVILLA Y LA BELLEZA A TODO

applications.explanationEn: Mira is the positive command for one familiar listener and calls for attention.
Olvida supplies the positive informal command and lo is attached for the thing to forget.
Lo attaches to the affirmative tú command olvida, and the written accent preserves the original stress.

applications.exampleEs: EL PROBLEMA DE LOS CIENTÍFICOS ES QUE
applications.explanationEn: El problema opens the frame, the de phrase identifies whose problem it is, and es que introduces the situation.
Veis is the informal plural vosotros form for the several people addressed, used mainly in Spain.

applications.exampleEs: LE VEIS LA MARAVILLA Y LA BELLEZA A TODO
applications.explanationEn: Le marks the perceived entity before veis; maravilla and belleza name the qualities, and a todo makes that entity explicit.
Se marks moverse: the organism itself is moving.
Quiere changes for one subject, and abrazar stays in its dictionary form with te attached.
Te attaches to abrazar and marks one familiar person as the recipient of the hug.
Qué keeps its accent because it introduces an exclamation of degree.

cards.questionEn: How do you introduce the situation that is causing a problem?
cards.noteEn: El problema names the difficulty, es identifies it, and que introduces the situation that follows. A de phrase may be inserted after problema to say whose problem it is.

example.es: El problema es que no tenemos tiempo.
example.en: The problem is that we do not have time.

cards.noteEn: Here científicos is a plural noun naming people who do science, not an adjective meaning “scientific.”

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; part of es que
no separate English word; part of es que
may have no separate English word; marks the thing receiving the effect
cards.noteEn: Le can appear before a verb even when a later phrase beginning with a names the receiver explicitly. English normally states that receiver only once.

example.es: Le cambié la rueda al coche.

cards.promptEs: me/te/le/nos/os/les + quitar + cosa (+ a alguien o algo)
cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone takes one thing away from another person or thing?
cards.answerEn: Use a short word such as me or le with quitar, then name the thing taken away. You can add a followed by the person or thing that is deprived of it.
cards.noteEn: Quitar changes for the person and time. The short word identifies the person or thing that loses something: me, te, le, nos, os, or les. With an unchanged dictionary-form verb, attach it as in quitarle; with a changed verb, place it before, as in le quita or me quitaste. Spanish can repeat or clarify the affected entity after a, even though English uses ‘from’ or a possessive. In the prompt, each plus sign means ‘followed by,’ and the parentheses mark the optional clarifying phrase.

example.es: Ana le quita el juguete a Luis.
example.en: Ana takes the toy away from Luis.

cards.noteEn: Quitáis is the present form used with informal plural vosotros, common in Spain.

cards.questionEn: How does Spanish in Spain address several people informally?
cards.answerEn: Use vosotros or vosotras forms, such as vuestro for “your” and podéis for “you all can.”
cards.noteEn: Vosotros addresses a mixed or all-male group; vosotras addresses an all-female group. These forms are common in Spain. Most of Latin America uses ustedes instead, with different verb and possessive forms.

example.en: You all can bring your books.

cards.promptEs: moho mucilaginoso · vómito de perro · abrazo
cards.answerEn: The characters admire a slime mold until its dog-vomit nickname and autonomous movement make the encounter grotesquely affectionate.
cards.noteEn: The organism is discussed with genuine scientific enthusiasm and claims about pigment and zinc resistance. The joke repeatedly collides that analytical wonder with its appearance, its crude nickname, and the final suggestion that the moving blob wants a hug.

cards.answerEn: from; introduces the person or thing something is taken from
cards.noteEn: After quitarle, a can introduce or clarify the person or thing that loses something. Natural English uses ‘from’ even though Spanish uses a.

example.es: Le quitan el balón a Pablo.
example.en: They take the ball away from Pablo.

cards.noteEn: Al is the required contraction of a + el. Spanish writes them as one word whenever both occur together.

cards.answerEn: Use al followed by the action verb in its dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Al + verb tells when the main action happens. Translate it naturally as “when,” “on,” or “upon”: al llegar means “when arriving” or simply “when someone arrives.”
cards.questionEn: How do you say “when doing something” or “upon doing something”?

example.en: When I arrive, I will call you.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that someone tries to do an action?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of intentar followed directly by the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: No linking preposition is needed between the two verbs. Intento abrir means “I try to open,” and intentamos salir means “we try to leave.” The attempted action stays in its basic -ar, -er, or -ir form.

example.en: We try to open the window.

cards.noteEn: Analizar stays in its unchanged dictionary form, and las attaches to represent the feminine plural things being analyzed.

example.es: Necesito analizar las muestras; voy a analizarlas mañana.
example.en: I need to analyze the samples; I am going to analyze them tomorrow.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.
Tío literally means “uncle,” but in casual speech in Spain it can address a male friend much like “dude” or “man.”

example.es: Tío, no me lo puedo creer.

cards.noteEn: In slime molds, plasmodios are the creeping, multinucleate stages of the organism.

example.es: Los plasmodios se desplazan hacia el alimento.

cards.questionEn: What is the Spanish term for “slime mold”?
cards.noteEn: Moho means mold and mucilaginoso means slimy, but together they are the conventional Spanish name for a slime mold, a group of amoeba-like organisms rather than ordinary fungus.

example.es: El moho mucilaginoso vive en lugares húmedos.
example.en: Slime mold lives in damp places.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.noteEn: Mucilaginoso literally means slimy or mucilaginous. In moho mucilaginoso it forms the conventional Spanish name for a slime mold.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.noteEn: After a form of haber, aumentado is aumentar’s completed-action form.

cards.answerEn: look; listen; hey (to get someone's attention)
cards.noteEn: Mira is the positive command form of mirar used with one familiar person. At the start of a comment, it often simply gets the listener's attention, like “look,” “listen,” or “hey,” without asking them to look at an object.

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.
Amarillo changes its ending to match what it describes: amarillo, amarilla, amarillos, or amarillas.
Esto is a neutral demonstrative for an unidentified thing, fact, or whole situation. It is not used directly before a noun.

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something makes a person or thing become a certain way?
cards.answerEn: Use a matching form of hacer, then the affected person or thing, then the word that describes the resulting quality.
cards.noteEn: Hacer changes for the person and time. The affected person or thing can be a noun or a short object word such as me, te, lo, la, los, or las. The final describing word agrees with what it describes: resistente becomes resistentes for a plural object.
Resistentes is plural to match the things that have this resistance.

example.es: Estas plantas son resistentes al frío.
example.en: These plants are resistant to cold.

cards.noteEn: Increíble has the same form for a masculine or feminine singular subject. Its plural is increíbles.
Placed after a comment, eh can turn it into a casual request for the listener to agree. This differs from hesitation eh, meaning ‘uh,’ or an attention-getting ‘hey.’
Ja represents a short burst of laughter in writing.

cards.promptEs: ser para identidad · estar para ubicación
cards.questionEn: Which Spanish “to be” verb says what something is, and which says where it is?
cards.answerEn: Use ser for identity or a defining description; use estar for the location of a person or thing.
cards.noteEn: This contrast is not simply permanent versus temporary. Forms of ser such as soy and es identify or describe what something is. Forms of estar such as están normally locate people and things. Events are a common exception: Spanish uses ser to say where or when an event takes place.

example.es: El museo es famoso y está en Madrid.
example.en: The museum is famous and is in Madrid.

cards.noteEn: Mola is an informal expression common in Spain for saying that something is cool or appealing.
Olvida is the positive informal command for one listener, and lo attaches for the thing to forget. The written accent keeps the original stress.

example.en: If it does not work, forget it.

cards.promptEs: imperativo afirmativo de tú + pronombre al final
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the command and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: A positive command tells someone to do something, rather than not to do it. With one informal listener, sienta + te becomes siéntate. A written accent may be added so the combined word keeps the original stress. In a negative command, the short word goes before the verb instead: no te sientes.
cards.questionEn: If a positive command includes a short word such as te (“yourself”) or lo (“it”), where does that word go?

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks the person or thing in which a quality is perceived
cards.noteEn: In verle una cualidad a alguien o algo, le marks one person or thing and les marks more than one. It appears before a changed form of ver or attaches to ver in its unchanged dictionary form. Natural English usually expresses the same relation with ‘in.’

example.en: I see a future in the project.

cards.promptEs: verle una cualidad a alguien o algo
cards.questionEn: How do you say that you see a quality in someone or something?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of ver with le or les, name the quality, and optionally clarify the person or thing with a.
cards.noteEn: Ver changes for the person and time: for example, veo, ves, or veis. With a changed form, put le for one entity or les for more than one before the verb. Name the perceived quality next; a can then introduce the person or thing explicitly. Natural English usually rearranges this as ‘see a quality in someone or something.’

example.es: Le veo mucho potencial a esta idea.
example.en: I see a lot of potential in this idea.

cards.noteEn: Veis is the present form of ver for informal plural vosotros, common in Spain.

example.en: Do you all see that light?

cards.answerEn: in; introduces the person or thing in which a quality is perceived
cards.noteEn: After verle una cualidad, a can introduce or clarify the person or thing associated with that quality. Natural English usually rearranges the idea and uses ‘in.’

example.es: Le veo un defecto al plan.
example.en: I see a flaw in the plan.

cards.noteEn: Dios names God, but said by itself it can also react to surprise, excitement, frustration, or strong nostalgia. The tone decides whether natural English keeps ‘God’ or uses an exclamation such as ‘man.’

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks moverse, “to move”
cards.noteEn: With mueve, se shows that the organism itself moves.
Mueve is the present form of mover for one person or thing. With se, it means that thing moves itself.
Quiere is the present form of querer for one person or thing. Before another verb in its dictionary form, it expresses what that subject wants to do.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone wants to do?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of querer, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Querer changes to match the person and time, while the desired action stays unchanged: quiero salir, quieres comer, queremos dormir. Spanish does not insert a between the two verbs.
Abrazar stays in its unchanged dictionary form, and te attaches for one familiar person being hugged.

cards.answerEn: how (to what a degree, as in qué insoportable)
cards.noteEn: Qué before an adjective can express a strong degree, like English “how” in “how strange!” It keeps its written accent.

cards.answerEn: Write qué, cómo, cuándo, and similar words with an accent when they ask a question or add an exclamation.
cards.noteEn: This includes direct questions (¿Qué quieres?), questions inside another sentence (No sé qué quiere), and exclamations (¡Qué bonito!). Without the accent, these words usually connect parts of a sentence instead: el libro que quiero means “the book that I want.”
cards.questionEn: Why do words such as que, como, and cuando sometimes have a written accent?
